speechtext: It is an error in the memorandum to council.

I do not know. It may have been in the report or in the copying of the order. In any case we had no intention of making the contract for a longer period than five years or for a larger quantity than
125.000	tons. With that 125,000 tons, and the 20.000 tons we got last year and the year before, we shall have a total of 145,000 tons of new rails which will be laid upon the Intercolonial Railway. When this is .done as I have said, there will be 149 miles of the road not re-railed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I am unable to see how the hon. gentleman makes it 125,000 tons. It says 50,000 tons for the first year, and
25.000	tons a year for four years thereafter.
We only get 25,000 tons the first year.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: And for five years thereafter.
\D CANALS. No, that is not the arrangement.

Is there any other binding arrangement with the company ?
The MINISTER OF RAH, VAYS AND CANALS. No, there is no other arrangement between the parties. We had not it in contemplation to make an arrangement for a longer term than five years or a greater quantity than 125,000 tons.

Before the hon. gentleman passes from that point, I desire to ask a question. In the report of the inspector, contained in the last report of the chief engineer on the Intercolonial Railway, it is stated that there are 1,315 miles of main road, and 271 miles of freight branches and wharfs. I do not suppose he intends to lay the freight branches and wharfs with the 80-pound rails ?
No.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Then that would leave on the main line from Montreal to Halifax 840 miles. Moncton to St. John 89 miles, Truro to Sydney 270 miles, and North Sydney branch, 5 miles. If I understood the hon. gentleman right, he states that there are 80 miles on the Cape Breton road laid. Then, there are 30 miles on the Truro branch laid, or a total of 110. Does the hon. gentleman intend to lay again the Drummond County Railway with the 80-pound rails ?
Not where it has been laid with 70-lb. rails.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: How many miles have been laid with 70-lb. rails ?
Forty-three.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That would leave 1,022 miles to be laid yet.

The hon. gentleman does not include the short line that we propose to lay. We propose to lay from Montreal to Halifax, from Moncton to St. John, from Truro to Sydney, from New Glasgow to Pictou Landing, from Pugwash Junction to Pug-wash, from Stellarton Junction to Ferrona Junction, from Oxford Junction to Pictou, from North Sydney to Sydney, including the Dartmouth branch and some other sections, making altogether 1,315 miles. We propose to double track 37 miles in addition.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: You have nothing to do between Montreal and St. Rosalie ?

We propose to lay the whole

Drummond County line with the exception of the 43 miles.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That is from St. Rosalie to Point Levis ?

If the hon. gentleman deducts from the 840 miles, the 39 miles from Montreal to Ste. Rosalie, he gets the actual mileage. It will be subject to the reduction by the distance between Montreal and Ste. Rosalie. That would be 110 miles short of providing for the whole line.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Axe there any other lines than those I mentioned ? There is from Montreal to Halifax S40 miles, that is exclusive of the Ste. Rosalie branch. From Moncton to St. John, 89 miles, from Truro to Sydney, 270 miles, from Sydney to North Sydney, 5 miles.

The hon. gentleman did not include the branch from New Glasgow to Pictou Landing, he did not include the line from Pugwasli Junction tol Pugwasli, from Stellarton Junction to Ferrona Junction, nor from Oxford Junction to Pictou, a distance of 70 miles. There are some other portions of the line which we did not contemplate laying with new rails.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman intends to relay the New Glasgow branch and all the branches near the Intercolonial Railway with 80-pound rails ?
All those I have named we propose to relay.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Why do you have to double the line on the Intercolonial Railway with 80-pound rails ? The New Glasgow branch would do with the other rails, and these branches to the different little places would do with G7-pound rails.

We do not propose to lay any of those portions at as early a date as the portions I have described, but we propose to lay them later on, after we have exhausted the quantity we now ask authority to purchase. But anything short of these portions will not put the line in the shape it ought to be in for the reason that these portions are all used for the carriage of considerable freight; heavy locomotives and heavy trains wiill pass over those lines, and we will have to put them in equally good condition as the other portions of the line. After we have done these we will still have 110 miles for which no provision has been made. Now the ihon. gentleman asked me yesterday to bring to the committee a copy of the telegram which we sent from the department to Mr. Clergue with reference to the contract which had been forwarded to him. I have a copy of it here which I Mr. BLAIR.
will read in order that it may go upon the 1 Hansard' :
Ottawa, April 12th, 1901.
F. H. Clergue,
President Lake Superior Power Co.,
Sault Ste. Marie, Ont.
Please return draft contracts for rails by tonight's mail; they were inadvertently forwarded to you without minister haying seen them.
(Sgd.) L. K. JONES,
Secretary.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Have yon an answer to that ?

No, but we received an answer during my absence somewhat different from the one which we hoped to receive, an answer dated the 15th of April, from Philadelphia, from the president of the Lake Superior Power Company, returning to us the contract executed by them. The contract which they had returned executed, is the same document in all respects as the one, a copy of which was placed either upon tlie Table or in the hands of the hon. gentleman in the earlier portion of the discussion. It is signed by the Lake Superior Power Company, hut it has not been executed by me. I have the letter, dated April 15tli to the following effect;
L. K. Jones, Secretary, Department Railways and Canals, Ottawa.
I take pleasure in inclosing to you herewith contract duly executed in duplicate by the president and vice-president of this company between the Minister of Railways and Canals and the Lake Superior Power Company for a supply of steel rails.
I remain yours, very truly,
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
President.
This is the draft of the contract which provided for a supply of rails for five years, the draft that was laid on the Table, and it is in that unexecuted form so far as the department is concerned, which it was in when the papers were handed to the hon. gentleman the other night.
And the proposals which were mentioned in the correspondence ?

Yes, I have the former proposal here from the Lake Superior Power Company, dated June 8th, 1900, to which I made reference the first day of the discussion. It is a lengthy document, and I will send it over <to the hon. gentleman. It may be considered as laid on the Table.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What does the minister propose to do with the agreement now signed by the company ?

I propose to have an agreement drawn that will be in strict accordance with the order in council. I propose to have that

document sent to the company for their execution. I have no doubt at all hut that the document so drawn will be executed, lit has not yet been prepared, but I have no doubt it will be satisfactory to the company if it is in accordance with the order in council.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There is no doubt, apparently, that the document that is executed by the company is absolutely in accordance with the terms that the company understood they were making with the government.

I do not know what they may have understood. I know that they were in possession of a copy of the order in council. The order in council was sent to them immediately upon its having been passed by council, agreeable to the request which Mr. Clergue made. He was not, apparently, particular about the contract. He was content that he should know what council was prepared to do, and if he had been very solicitous about the contract, I suppose we would have heard him calling for the contract. Some reference was made last evening by the hon. member for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) to the question of the price at which the government were contracting to purchase these rails. I have made a statement on the sub.iect. and I propose, even now, with the forbearance of the committee
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Before the hon. minister goes away from that subject, I would like to ask him if the return of the signed contract is the only response that has been received to the telegram that was sent on the 12th instant ?

It is the only response I have seen, and my deputy tells me that he has received no letter from them. I want to make reference again to the question of the market price of rails extending over a period prior and subsequent to the date of the arrangement with Mr. Clergue.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Before you proceed with the discussion of that, the hon. gentleman promised to lay on the Table of the House the information that I asked for, as to the form in which steel rails, taken up from the road, were credited, whether they went into store account and were credited to the revenue account, or in what manner were they credited.

There is nothing that I can lay on the Table in respect to that, but, I stated to the hon. gentleman that the new rails that were purchased by us were charged to capital, less the amount of the old rails, which went into store account. That is the system which is pursued by the department, and as I understand, the system which has been pursued by the department
whenever rails have been got on capital account.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What I want to know especially is, when they went into store account, to what were they credited ?
Do you want to know what amount was credited ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What amount was credited, and to what account they were credited ?
They were credited to capital account. The difference between the amount in respect to the old rails and the amount which the new rails cost is the only amount which is charged up to capital.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: At what price were the old rails credited to capital account when they were taken off the road ?

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What is done with the old rails ? How7 are they disposed of ? Are they left in store, or are they sold and a price obtained for them ?
They will be sold, of course.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: They have not been sold ?

They are being sold from time to time. I made a very full statement the other day in regard to that. A good many of the small roads that are being constructed under government contract buy their rails from us when we have a good quality of rails for them.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Would the hon. minister allow' me to refer again to the matter of the Clergue contract ? I understand the hon. minister to say that Mr. Clergue did not send any reply or response to the telegram except the contract that has been returned signed. Are W'e to understand from the minister that he is in a position to say that no response has been received by his department other than the contract returned signed ?

I am not in a position to say one w7ay or the other at the present moment. I understand from the deputy that lie is quite confident that there is no letter on the subject further than the one I have just read, but he will ascertain whether there is any other.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Then, wre are to understand, as far as appears at the present time, that the power company propose to

hold the government to the contract as sent to them for signature, or the five years contract.

I do not imagine that the power company are going to raise the slightest question with us as to the contract that they will enter into. The power company, I am sure, will unhesitatingly execute 'such a contract as we will draw in conformity with the terms of the order in council. Nothing has been said, no communication has been received from the company which would justify me in inferring that they will raise the slightest objection to the execution of the contract in conformity with the order in council.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Has the hon. gentleman notified the company, since he received that communication, that he is not going to accept the contract ? I understand on the 15th he was advised they had signed this contract, nine or ten days ago. Has the hon. gentleman communicated to them that he does not propose to accept the contract as executed by them ?

I have not seen Mr. Clergue, but I expected to have seen him personally. I was about writing to him on the subject, but I understood he was coming here today, and I intended to have some conversation with him. There has been no letter sent from the department.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Would the hon. minister explain to the committee, as I think it would be probably interesting to them to know, why it was, that yesterday, when this matter was before the committee for discussion, it was not mentioned at that time by the minister that the contract had been returned signed ?

The contract came back while I was absent, and as a matter of fact, I was not aware at the moment that the contract had been returned executed by these gentlemen. It is here now, and you see to what extent it has been executed. You see that it has not been executed by me, and it will not be executed by me, nor will a contract be executed by me unless and until it is in conformity with the order in council that has been passed.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Did the hon. minister have any communication from Mr. Clergue on the subject except the returned contract-any letter with the returned contract ?
No. I understand not further than the one I have just read.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Just simply inclosing the contract.
This is the original paper. I will pass it over and the hon. gentleman will see it, but I would like him to take care of it.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I thought you said you had some communication from the president of the company in Philadelphia. This is it ?

Yes. Now, I stated to the committee the other day that I had not gone through the sources of information, showing just what the prices were which rule in the market for rails either in the United States or England, until recently. I have had one of the officers of my department do so very carefully and I shall impart to the committee the information which these papers disclose. First let me call attention to the price of rails in the United States, because something has been said by gentlemen opposite on that question. It will be found by referring to the Monthly Summary of Commerce and Finance of the United States, which contains the record of the price Oif steel rails from day to day. The price of steel rails in the United States on the 25th of July, 1900, was $35. That price of $35 ruled continuously and uninterruptedly until the 12tli of September, when the price fell to $30, and the price continued at $30 until the 2Gth of September, when it fell again to $26, and down again until the 17th of April, the last date for which I have the figures, the price has remained uninterruptedly at $26. The committee will have in mind, I apprehend, that this arrangement was made by the government with Mr. Clergue in the month of August last. The order in council did not pass until the 9th of October, founded upon the recommendation whch was sent by me to council, dated the 26th of September, but the arrangement was made in August. Mr Clergue was pressing to have us agree, if we were prepared ito agree, upon terms which would be sufficient to induce him to establish this industry, and we gave him to understand in August that we had determined upon it and he was then in a position, relying upon the conclusion at which the council had informally arrived, to make the preliminary arrangement.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Were these oral or written ?

The communications that I am now speaking of were verbal, because the gentleman was here himself to hear what would be determined upon. We had to come to an arrangement with him then because it appeared to be important that no 'time should be lost. I was in a position to assure him that the order in council would in due course be passed in accordance with the arrangement. We settled upon

the price and we settled upon the terms which we would agree with him upon. We settled as to the term of years upon the first year's definite contract and upon the four years' continuous subsequent contract, making for the five years in all 125,000 tons. At that time, you will observe that the price of rails in the United States market, and until the 12th of the following month, was $35 a ton.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: When did the minister say he fixed the price with Mr. Clergue ?
In August.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It is very curious that on the 29th of September the only offer made form England to Canada for steel rails ; the only inquiry made from this country as far as I can find out, was made on the 29th of September, asking the price of 80-pound steel rails in England. The reply to that cable was : ' Delivered in Montreal, $32.24.'

I do not know what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Osier) may be referring to, and I do not know what his statement is based upon, but I do not see the particular relevancy of that observation. The arrangement, as I tell the hon. gentleman, was made in the month of August, and it is so recorded in the order in council which passed on the 9th of October.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Does that order in council give the price of the rails ?
Yes, Sir.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The order in council of the 9th of October, does.
The or-|der in council of the 9th of October was the only order in council actually passed.

I am saying that that order in council contains a statement which the members of the council individually and collectively would know, to this effect :
This subject was, however, discussed informally by the cabinet towards the close of August, 1900, being favourably considered, and it was understood that a recommendation would be made and be submitted by the Minister of Railways and Canals on the basis of a contract for 25,000 tons to be supplied in 1901 at $32.60 a ton, the price then being paid by the Department of Railways and Canals under its then rail contract.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What time in August was that ?

Towards the close of August. It does not say what particular date it was. It was one of the meetings of the council which took place at the latter end of August.
It must have been about the 22nd or 23rd of August, because I was present and I did not return to Canada until the 20th or 21st. I came immediately to Ottawa, so that it would be almost immediately after that. There was no record of council to show just what date it was, because it was an informal debate which settled the terms and on the strength of which-I do not think I wrote him-one of my colleagues may have written to him. But I know I stated to Mr. Clergue the first opportunity 'I had of seeing him after this date, that the matter was settled and agreed upon, and it would only be a question of drawing out the necessary papers and having the recommendation go to council for the order to be passed upon it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If I understand the minister aright, there was a memorandum prepared in August which was filed in his department in reference to the agreement.
No, there was not. There was no memorandum prepared in the department until September, and the date of that memorandum was the 26th of September.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I do not mean the memorandum to council. There was no note or information filed in the department in reference to the oral or verbal agreement with Mr. Clergue in August, and the first that the department had notice of it was when they prepared the memorandum on the 26th of September.

I had notice of it, of course, in August. I do not know whether I had any conversation with the deputy minister on the subject at that time ; but there would be no record either in council or out of council on the subject. We had Mr. Clergue's application before us in the ordinary way of debate and discussion. We decided then which of Mr. Clergue's terms we would accede to. and which we would not accede to ; and the terms which we acceded to were stated in the order which was finally adopted on the 9th of October- that we would take from him 25,000 tons of rails, for the first year definitely, at $32.60 a ton, and for the four years following at a price which would depend on the English market.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What was the date on which Mr. Clergue made his proposal, and was it put in writing ?
The 8th of June.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is it understood that the power company will get a bonus on the rails that are made, in addition to the price that yon are paying ?
The subject of a bonus is not dealt with in this arrangement at all.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Do they get the bonus which the government gives for steel rails ?
There is no bonus on steel rails. There is a bonus on pig iron and on steel, and if they produce pig iron and steel, they will get a bonus on that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That will be $7 a ton more, which will bring it to about $41 a ton. We had better put it in that way before the country.

That is hardly a fair way to put it. The bonus on iron and steel would be paid anyway, even if this contract were not made. There is no bonus specifically on steel rails. There is a bonus on iron and steel, and if this company make iron and steel, they will undoubtedly get a bonus on that irrespective of this contract.
Does the Minister of Railways tell this House seriously that on the Oth' of August he made a contract with a company for 25,000 tons of rails ?
No, I did not say that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What I want to get at is the date on which the minister fixed the price to be paid for these rails.
The latter part of August.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Do you mean to say that this government made a verbal contract with the firm for 25,000 tons of rails at a price which the minister himself says was on a rising market ?
I said it was not on a falling market.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The minister said it was not on a falling market, and that the majority of people thought it was a rising market. Does the minister mean to say that he made a contract for
25,000	tons, and that he has not a scratch of the pen to show who was the man with whom he made the contract or the price agreed upon ? He has nothing but his own recollection of what occurred, which is repeated in an order in council adopted about six weeks afterwards, or on the 9tli of October. You cannot make this House believe that the Department of Railways is run in a manner like that. It is asking us to swallow too much. We have accepted a great deal, but I cannot believe it possible that any minister will quietly say that he made a verbal contract for $4,000,000 prac-Mr. ROBINSON (West Elgin).
tically, and fixed the price for $750,000 without having a scratch of the pen or a memorandum of the discussion as to the price. He does not know the date on which that conversation took place. He knows nothing about it except from recollection, that some time in the month of August a figure was agreed upon for the pui'chase.
I cannot believe that is possible.
I do not care very much whether the hon. gentleman believes it or not. I stated that in the latter part of August the members of this government, having this proposition of Mr. Clergue's before them
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is that proposition in writing ?
Yes, that proposition was in writing.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: As to the price on that date?

When he made his proposition in June, it was at the rate of $32 per ton. Later Mr. Clergue wanted a little more ; but we came to the conclusion that $32.00 was the very outside we would allow him. That was about the price at which rails were ruling at that time. We debated the question, and decided among ourselves which of the conditions Mr. Clergue sought to impose we would accede to, and it is a matter perfectly immaterial to me whether the hon. gentleman believes that or not.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It is quite evident that it is immaterial to the hon. gentleman and to the government what the opposition think, but it is not immaterial to the opposition. They settled the price at $32.G0 ; and yet Mr. Clergue did not get a letter from the government fixing the price in August or September. If that is the way contracts are made by the government, we would like to know it.
I understood the minister to say that the proposition of Mr. Clergue called for $32 a ton.
That was the original proposition in June.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Why was the increase of CO cents a ton added to that proposition ?

There was a number of things which Mr. Clergue urged us to accede to in connection with that proposition. One was to take 50,000 tons. We would not do that; we only agreed to take 25,000 tons. We proposed that the rails should be delivered not only at Montreal, but at Levis. We wanted some other conditions imposed, and we agreed to allow him $32.G0 a ton on his [DOT] being willing to make this arrangement with us, and to establish this industry.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Why did you give more than he asked ?

I am telling the hon. gentleman. He wanted more than $32 originally. He pointed out that the price of rails was as high as it had been at any time previous to that period. We agreed to give them the $32.60, the price we were paying for other rails, and he being willing to accept an arrangement with us, and deliver the 25,000 tons at Levis instead of, or as well as, at Montreal.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Had the market price gone up between June and August ?
I do not think so.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Yet he made a written proposition in June and you increased that in August.

Are we to understand that there is no record whatever of any conversation or understanding between the Minister of Railways and Mr. Clergue as to the price of rails, which conversation the minister alleges took place in the latter part of August, except the record of that conversation which is in the order in council that was passed on the 9th of October ? Is that correct 1	.
Yes, so far as my memory serves me.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: So that we have an order in council passed on the 9th of October, the day on which the writs for the election were issued, reciting the arrangement or understanding which took place in August previous, and we have nothing to verify that arrangement in any way except this order in council which, I assume, was dictated by the Minister of Railways on the 9th of October. In other words, the council got the facts from the Minister of Railways and passed an order in council, assuming that there was a previous arrangement made verbally by the Minister of Railways to the effect that $32.60 would be the price.
That is not a statement at all of the facts.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I would be glad to have the hon. gentleman's correct statement. The first portion of what I said, I understood, he admits is correct, namely, that there is no record of the verbal arrangement except what is contained in the order in council of the 9th of October, and that there is no way of verifying that verbal arrangement at present except the order In council. And I wish to follow that up by saying that there was no binding contract or obligation on the part of the government until the 9th of October, and that at that time-
There was no binding contract then.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There was no moral contract or obligation on the part of the government until the 9th of October, and at that time I presume we are justified in assuming that the government was well aware of the fact that the prices of steel rails had fallen from $35 to $30 on the 12th of September, and had fallen from $30 to $26 per ton before this contract was made, so that there was every indication to the government that the price of steel rails was then coming down.

I would not assent to my hon. friend's statement that there was no moral obligation until the 9tli of October. The minister has stated that in the latter part of August- he has not been able to fix the exact date- the matter was discussed and agreed to in council. Hon. gentlemen who have been members of council know that it is a common practice to have some matter discussed and the policy thereon adopted in council, and then the minister in charge of the department interested gives expression to that policy by formulating a report which shall be the basis of an order in council. This matter having been agreed to in August, the Minister of Railways would naturally follow it up in due course with a report. It appears that this report was not formally made until September. That would go over to council and be deposited in a box with perhaps fifty or a hundred others and it might remain there a considerable time if no attention were called to it. I was not here in October, but in a distant part of the Dominion, hut knowing the practice of council, I can understand that that report made in September, and the order in council drafted thereon would remain in a pile with others until attention was drawn to it. But the moral obligation unquestionably existed in August if the minister, as he said, then made an agreement with Mr. Clergue and fixed the prices and conditions.
We want that letter down.

There was no letter. The Minister of Railways says he told Mr. Clergue personally. If the minister in August came to an arrangement with Mr. Clergue and fixed the prices, the mere fact that he delayed several weeks making his report and the further fact that several weeks elapsed before the report was endorsed by an order in council, should not prejudice Mr. Clergue. The transaction was settled in August, and, therefore, we are dealing with it on the prices that prevailed in August.
When the matter was discussed in council and a policy adopted, would there not be a record of that ?

Not until the minister drew up a report and submitted it. It would be his duty to give expression to the conclusion reached by council in the form of a report. That report would then be translated into an order in council. But up to that moment there would be no record of the agreement except as between the Minister of Railways and Mr. Clergue.
Would not that report be still available ?

It has been read. The order in council is a mere echo of the report. Both documents have been laid before the House.
Hon. Mr. HAGGAItT. I would like the Minister of Railways to explain this. On the 23rd of April addressing this House he said :	.
But the difficulty about the contract was this : That it had never been executed and has not been executed to this day, and never came under my observation.

So, if what the hon. gentleman read appears to convey the impression that I said the contract which
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: had been sent to Mr. Clergue had not been signed down to that day, it did not convey what I intended to convey, because I could not tell what had been done by Mr. Clergue or by the Lake Superior Power Company with the contract which had been sent to them, until it had been brought back and had been brought to my notice.

Now, the hon. minister stated earlier in this discussion that he had no letter or telegram from the Lake Superior Power Company nor had he seen Mr. Clergue. Is he prepared to state that he had not seen any of the members of the firm and discussed this matter with them since the discussion in this House ?

I have not seen anybody who has any connection, as far as I know, with the Lake Superior Power Company. I have had no conversation with any such person on the subject. I am thoroughly confident in my own mind that the arrangement is satisfactory to Mr. Clergue. I know the understanding that we had with him, every member of the council knows that he was thoroughly satisfied to take the contract for a year, providing the order in council contained an assurance that we would continue it year after year. That was the distinct understanding in the various conversations he had with all the various members of the council-and I suppose there was hardly one member of the council he did not talk it over with. He met us in committee, a number together, and individually, and there wore many, many interviews before the matter was finally brought to a head. If you read the letter of the 8th of June, you will see that he wanted us to make some arrangement with regard to the tariff, and we had a good deal of discussion before we convinced him that we could not make any arrangement that would have any effect upon the tariff. Other features of this proposal were discussed between us-not between Mr. Clergue and myself alone, but between Mr. Clergue and every member of the council, certainly every active or leading member of it. And, when the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) says there is no record whatever with regard to this understanding that was arrived at, you cannot have any better record than the order in council. In the latter part of August, it was solemnly debated in council, though informally, and solemnly decided, that Mr. Clergue should have this contract for $32.60 per ton for a year. And on the strength of that-and I presume other members of the council may have given him the same information as I gave him-we were prepared to have the necessary papers drawn up and to enter into a contract with him. He went away thoroughly satisfied with that, and we liave in this order in council the declaration by the members of

tlie government that that had taken place. What better record do you want than that'/
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I understood the hon. minister to say that one member of the council gave him this information. Would he object to giving the name of the member who arranged the final details. 1 understood that he got the information from others
I think probably he did. But I am not going to mention names of other members of the council. I am pretty sure, however, that he must have got it from other members.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman on what date the Power Company attached their signature to the contract ?
I cannot tell that. It would be very recently.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Apparently it was on the 15th of April, I suppose-the date they sent the letter.
The day they attached the signature to the contract, the secretary had notified them to return it without attaching the signature.
My hon. friend knows that a telegram was sent on the 12th.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. minister notified them by telegraph to return the contract.
The secretary of the department notified them-acting under instructions.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: On the 15th they attached their signatures to it and returned it. It seems rather a strange thing that they did not return it without signing it.
Strange or not, that is the fact. Now I would like to make another statement. I have shown the prices for rails which ruled in the United States on these dates
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Before the hon. gentleman makes that statement, I would like to know if the committee is to understand that the essence of the whole arrangement with the Lake Superior Power Company was this : For 25,000 tons of rails for one year, that is 1901, at $32.60, and that for each and every year of the four years thereafter, there would be a contract made with the company for 25,000 tons each year to be governed by the price in England at the time the contract was made ; and that the arrangement for the following four years was as much of a contract, I mean, so far as an understanding was concerned, was as much of an understanding, as that there should be a contract for one year.
Yes, every bit.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
That is, that the hon. gentleman had agreed without the slightest reserve to take 125,000 tons of steel rails from the Lake Superior Power Company covering that period, and the only difference between that and making a contract at that time was that the four years contract was to be divided as there agreed, and prices fixed at the different periods. Then the committee is in possession of this fact, that the hon. gentleman was prepared to fulfil his word, and that he had bound us so far as his word was given, and it only required the form of writing to bind the Dominion of Canada hand and foot to a contract for
125,000	tons with the Lake Superior Power Company.
Yes, we would hold ourselves morally bound-
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
As to the prices will the hon. gentleman please explain Mr. Clergue's letter to him, in which he says :
American steel rails can be bad at $35 per ton free on board. 1 have myself purchased during the present season 85-pound steel rails for about

100 miles of track, and need an additional quantity. I have asked quotations from the principal American manufacturers, pointing out the fact that these rails were for export from the United States. You will note from the inclosed original communication from the Carnegie Steel Company works

I wish the hon. gentleman would bring that down, and that would fix the price of the rails.
-that these the largest manufacturers in the world, offer to fill our order for use in Canada at $32 per ton.
This the hon. gentleman had in his possession. The quotation, as he says, was $37 per ton in June last, while these parties who made the proposition to him were buying them at $32.

Well, I have said over and over again, that while prices in the United States held firm, as the quotations here show, there has always been a willingness to make a cut in order to capture the Canadian market, and I presume that what Mr. Clergue refers to here is just such a cut as is ,usual in that trade, not in rails alone, but Jin almost every branch of business. You can go and ask the Commissioner of Customs whether goods that are intended for export to Canada are not bought by people to pass through the customs house at prices at which they cannot be bought for consumption in the United States. The thing is constantly occurring, they do it in regard to rails as well as anything else. But does any one suggest that if it is im-'portant to encourage the establishment of a rail industry in Canada, we should allow ourselves to be stopped in the inception of such an enterprise because the United States manufacturers will cut below their market prices ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is it because the Americans make a cut in steel rails that the order in council specifies that the prices iu Great Britain should control the price ?

Yes, because we could never come to any agreement at all as to the future, nor agree to any mode of settling the question which would be fair to all parties unless we selected some market, and the English market is the only market we would [DOT]care to select.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I have just picked up a Bill *here, I do not know whose It Is or where 'it came from, which is worth calling attention to. It speaks of an Act respecting aid to Canadian railways passed by the Ontario legislature and read the third time on the 11th of April. The Ontario government have the same idea of fostering the steel rail industry in this country, but they evidently have not been in communication with the Minister of Railways, because they do not see the tremendous importance of fail-Mr. HAGGART.
ing to take advantage of a cut in American rails. This is a curious doctrine to come from a man who is representing a free trade side of the House, that he is not to buy in the cheapest market. However, the Ontario government put in a clause saying that the rails for any of these railways bonused by the government are to be of Canadian make, provided they are at the current price upon the open market in Great Britain or in the United States for rails of similar make and quality, the current freight rate added. That is the encouragement the Ontario government are giving, but this free trade government throw to the winds all idea of buying in a cheap market; they say, We will not have a cheap thing, we will have the dearest thing that we can get. The higher the better, evidently, because the Minister of Railways, in the papers he brings down, shows that Mr. Clergue offers to supply these rails at $32 a ton. The minister is asked why he gives $32.60. Oh ! he says, Mr. Clergue thought he had better have a little more. And the minister, knowing the election was just coming on, said : Well, 60 cents isn't much, it is only $15,000 altogether, that is a bagatelle, so we will call it $32.60.

we should fix for the first year the price that is to be paid ; take these quotations in either country, if you will, and ask yourselves whether you would not consider that the price we fix would be a fair price to agree upon, even if we did not have behind the undertaking, the desire and object of securing the establishment of this industry. The price would be a fair price.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: No.
I maintain it would. The hon. gentleman (Mir. Clancy) shakes has head.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I tell the hon. gentleman that has concluded his arrangement without a shadow of competition. In the first place, the proposition of a former parliament was to give encouragement to the manufacture of steel rails by way of a bonus that amounts, as my hon. friend from West Elgin (Mr. Robinson) said, to $6 a ton.
$7 a ton.

$7 a ton, including the grant of the province of Ontario. I am speaking of the encouragement given here. Now, this is separate and distinct from any thing that you may afterwards do in regard to steel rails. When parliament has given that encouragement it does not mean encouragement to a single industry in Canada. but it means encouragement to all. It is the duty of the government to buy their steel rails from Mr. Clergue or from anybody else as cheaply as they can, when the price is submitted to the test of competition. Surely the hon. gentleman does not pretend to say that he is obliged, after giving this ordinary encouragement to the Lake Superior Power Company to contract, as against every person else, after giving them the whole field of Canada as far as government railways are concerned, to give them high prices. The hon. gentleman evidently selected the very highest price he could get, because he stated here last night, during the debate, that his contract was not made when there was a falling market. He went so far as to say that he was then within
0	shillings of the highest price that had been paid for rails in England. Yet, he says this is a fair price. Let us see what means the hon. gentleman took to test the price on the open market in England. The hon. gentleman inquires of a firm in England what they are selling steel rails for. The very apt question would be: Do you want to buy ? No,
1	do not want to buy, I merely want to find out in order that I shall be able to fix the price on this side of the Atlantic. All that the hon. gentleman would have to do in future would be, as he has done in this case in the most studied manner, that is to select the highest price he can find in order to make a contract with Mr. Clergue. Mr. Clergue says : I am willing to take $32 a
ton for these rails, but, the minister persuades Mr. Clergue to make it 60 cents a ton more, and yet the hon. gentleman gets up and asks the committee to assent to the proposition, that this is a fair and reasonable amount for the department to pay. I never heard a bolder proposition made in or outside parliament.

In the event of any further sales in subsequent years of rails that may be offered in Great Britain not being up to the analysis, or exactly the same quality, would the hon. minister then feel that he was not called upon by the comparison of prices to regulate Mr. Clergue's price, because the words in the contract are 'of the same quality'? Will those words ' same quality,' be incorporated in the contract that you propose to substitute in place of this one ?

Certainly, we will have to get a good quality of steel rails. We certainly would not pay the same price for an inferior quality of rails that we would pay for a superior quality. We will have to get a quality of rail up to the standard that will be prescribed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
any one wlao lias followed the question at all knows that is the ease. Therefore, we did not attach much Importance to this particular feature, as I stated at the outset.
I do not anticipate that until the experiments have made greater progress than they have yet made, that there will be a satisfactory steel rail made which will contain nickel! I know that recent information which has been contained in late publications is to the effect that it has not yet been accomplished. I am sure that Mr. Clergue has not accomplished it, so that there will be no question in my mind as to the difference in value. If Mr. Clergue is able to produce and to furnish us with a fiist-class qualify of steel rail which will contain nickel, if Mr. Clergue can produce a better steel rail than the steel rails produced in England, he will do so without having any reasonable ground upon which to expect any higher price from us.

In the event of an analysis showing that there is a proportionate part, whether it is 2 or 4 per cent of nickel, in the rails produced by Mr. Oleigue, and then, in the further event ot the contract which will have to be substituted for this one incorporating these same words,
' game quality of rails,' what will happen then ? If Mr. Clergue says: My rails contain a certain proportion of nickel and the rails that you are subjecting me to compete against in Great Britain do not, then the minister will be bound by the contract if this term goes into the new contract.
No, I do not think so.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It seems to me that if the price of steel rails is enhanced by having a proportion of nickel in them, and it there are no nickel-steel rails in Great Britain there can be no competition, because they will not be of the same class.
If he gives us a better rail that cannot affect the price.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There must be some legal meaning attached to the words the same quality.' If you bind yourselves to these words in a contract, you cannot substitute an inferior quality, and it is admitted that the nickel rail is superior. Will these words be incorporated in the new agreement which, I understand, is to be prepared .
We have not drafted the agreement yet. I cannot say what we will put into it, but we will fully safeguard the public interests.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What about Mr. Cler-gne's interests ?

He will come after the public interests.
lion. Mr. HAGGART. On the 10th of April last, the minister declared in the House that the ores in the neighbourhood of Michipicoten contained 2 or 3 per cent of nickel.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That was what I understood.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Well, it was news to every one in this part of the country. The minister stated that we would get a superior kind of rail from Mr. Clergue, but where the minister got that information I do not know. Mr. Clergue says no such tiling in his proposition. He says that the ores are to be taken from the north shore of Lake Superior, that he will make that ore into steel, but he does not say one word about nickel. He says he is going to purchase Sudbury nickel to incorporate in the steel, and if he does that he hopes the minister will take a certain proportion of these for grades and other parts of the road, but he will require $10 more a ton than for the other rail. The minister concealed-I will not say wilfully-but he seemed to be entirely ignorant of the communication he received from Mr. Clergue. Mr. Clergue does not say that in the rails he intends to furnish to the minister there will be a particle of nickel. What he says is that the industry of making rails in which nickel is incorporated is to be the future industry in that portion of the country, and on account of the superiority of these rails there will be an immense demand for them, but if the minister takes them it is on the condition that he will pay $10 more a ton for them. The minister tries to make the House and the country believe that he has made a bargain for a less sum of money than the market price at the time he made the bargain. But, why does he quote prices in England in June, July, September and October, when he has in his possession a letter from the Carnegie Steel Works, offering the same rails to Mr. Clergue for a less price than the minister pays for them ?
You are referring to the letter of June 8.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I read it before, and I will read it again :
The present market quotation for steel rails in the United States is $37 a ton, but within a week it has been intimated that by private negotiations for a large contract American steel rails can be had for $35 a ton. I have myself purchased during the present season 85-pound steel rails for about 100 miles of track, and needing an additional quantity I have asked quotations from the principal American manufacturers pointing out the fact that these rails were for export from the United States. You will note from the inclosed communication from the Carnegie Steel Company

I have asked the minister to bring down that communication.

-that these, largest manufacturers in the world offered to fill our order for use In Canada at $32 a ton, a reduction of $5 below the published quotation.
The inference to be drawn from that is, that you can make an arrangement by private agreement in the United States to get these rails for exportation to Canada for $5 a ton less than the quoted market price. There are several propositions made by Mr. Clergue, and in reference to nickel, he says :
To be sent back to Canada in the form of nickel-steel in competition with Canada's manufactures is so gross an injustice that any statesman regardful of the interests of his country should feel justified in taking the most radical steps to remedy the injustice. But the method proposed is in no sense radical and cannot offend the judgment of the most radical free trader. It simply offers the United States an opportunity for an equal and fair exchange in the commodity concerned. But such nickel-steel rails as the government may require for curves we will furnish at an advance of $10 per ton over the price of ordinary steel.
It, therefore, will be seen, if the minister gets the nickel rails, he will have to pay $10 extra for them. The minister says he has not entered Into a contract yet. Is he going to make his contract in the words of the order in council of the 9th of October last ?
In accordance with that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: We have at least the right to get from the minister a copy of the proposed contract which he intends to enter into with Mr. Clergue before we vote this sum of nearly $4,000,000. We should know what terms he intends to offer in that contract. If the terms are confined to the ipsissima verba of the order in council, surely the minister can to-morrow produce the proposed contract which he intends to enter into with Mr. Clergue.

There is very grave doubt as to whether Mr. Clergue will be able to make delivery of this year's rails, and I would ask the minister if the contract is to be moved on for one year ? Is the price that is fixed for this year's rails to govern the price of the first delivery, and then the contract to proceed as contemplated for the following four years ?

The question as to whether the contract will be moved on is a question perhaps to be determined by the Governor in Council. It has not yet reached the stage at which it became necessary to pass upon that question, and I am not in a position to say what the conclusion of council will be. We will, however, keep steadily in our minds the importance of encouraging the establishment of this industry. We will take no step that will tend to defeat or destroy that object; and in doing so we will 1184
take care that the public interest shall be fully safeguarded, and that we keep ourselves within the terms of the order in council that has been passed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Was the minister aware at the time this contract was made that the Dominion Iron and Steel Company of Sydney proposed to establish a plant for the purpose of manufacturing steel rails 7

I can state to the hon. gentleman that I not only was not aware of it, but I am satisfied in my own mind that the Dominion Iron and Steel Company had not it in contemplation at that time, either in October or in August. I am absolutely certain that they had not spoken of it in the month of August
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman has stated that the government would take good care, in the event of the Lake Superior Power Company being unable to furnish the rails as provided under the contract, that nothing would be done to destroy that industry. Does he mean the committee to understand that if that company had to accept the current price for rails, that would destroy the industry ?

If it becomes necessary to revise the arrangement and to extend it, then the question of price would have to be a matter for consideration. The government are not going to pay the Lake Superior Power Company more than a fair and proper price according to the state of the market. If the supply of rails is not made this year as contracted for, but is postponed by the action of the government or by the action of the company, the price would be a matter subject to reconsideration and revision. I have no hesitation in saying that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Will the price at which the Dominion Iron and Steel Company can produce these rails have any effect on the price which the government will pay the Clergue Company in the succeeding four years ?

The arrangement is based on the price of rails in England which is a reasonably steady market, and a market which will give us a guarantee that we shall not pay more than a fair and proper price. I am not prepared to say what elements would enter into the consideration of the Governor in Council in settling the price. If the Dominion Steel Company were manufacturing rails,' I am not sure but that might be a very proper matter to consider. I do not want, however, to make any statement on that subject at this time.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman has not yet answered my hon. friend from South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Hag-
I have stated over and over again that the contract to be drawn up will give effect to and be in accordance with the order in council.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman is speaking a little too hurriedly. I was about to state that criticism may show that the contract which the hon. gentleman will eventually draw up will not be in terms of the order in council.

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: And it is a matter on -which the opposition has a right to criticise the government if it is not drawn in terms of the order in council. I pointed out yesterday to the hon. gentleman that the present practice in England is that all contracts of this kind should be made with the stipulation that they should not be binding until parliament has approved of them. The hon. gentleman made a contract in October last, but the formal contract has not yet been drawn up, and he asks the House to vote the supply for that contract. The House, I think, is reasonably entitled to see the form of the contract at least, under the peculiar circumstances ot this case. I expressed some doubt yesterday as to whether we had all the facts. It turns out now that we had not all the facts yesterday, because the hon. gentleman certainly led the House to believe yesterday that this contract had not been executed by the company at all.
That is not the statement I intended to make to the committee, because the contract was sent some time ago.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I want to show the hon. gentleman how easily misapprehensions arise. I did not mean to state that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

There is no objection.

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
